newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK air cargo business to Korea on upturn.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK air cargo business to Korea on upturn.

text.p: After months in the doldrums, the ex-UK to Korea airfreight market has begun to show signs of an upturn in fortunes, a Reuters survey shows.

It also indicates that London-Japan, which prospered in terms of cargo yields and volumes for at least a year up to the beginning of this month, appears to have recovered from a short fortnight-long downturn in business.
Frank Smith, UK cargo sales head of Korean Air, said that his trading to Seoul had been poor since January but had begun to revive from June 12.
"Earlier that week, bookings were so slow that I gave away 30 tonnes of my ex-UK capacity to our German station, which had been doing better," he recalled.
"But then calls and bookings began coming in from people I hadn't heard from for months. I ended up with a 50 tonnes' backlog I still have to clear," he said.
Japan Airlines' UK cargo sales manager Tony Edwards noted that after long-term UK-Japan cargo success, "at the start of June, bookings on the route just died.
"But is appears to have been just a two week quiet period, a 'blip'. I dont know why it happened, it just illustrates what an unpredictable business this is," he said.
Smith was also puzzled as to exactly why the sudden turnaround in his main market had happened.
But he believed it had much to do with reports of the South Korean government beginning to ease its frugality campaign which was aimed at reducing the country's current account deficit.
"From what I have heard from Seoul bcgousiness contacts, this is making available more money available for Koreans to spend on imports," he noted.
Edwards said that much of the freight JAL was carrying from Britain to Japan comprised finished computer products.

KAL's Smith said that his UK-Tokyo loads had also picked up "dramatically" of late and similarly pointed to a recent hefty rise in his carrier's computer cargo business from the British Isles - particularly Ireland - to Japan.
"Last week I got a 25-tonne computer order for Tokyo, which was the biggest we've seen of its type for some time," he stated.

Additionally, he said that while KAL's Britain-China cargo volumes had been "steady" since the beginning of 1997, there had lately been an increase in mobile 'phone and broadcasting-related shipments to the Shenzhen economic zone.

China Eastern Airlines' cargo business from Britain to China is presently "inconsistent, due to the strength of the pound affecting exports", reported Ashraf Salama, of its UK cargo general sales agent, Jet Link.

He noted a switch by some Chinese importers from air to seafreight to reduce costs when speed of delivery was not absolutely paramount. As a result, his carrier had recently lost two possible 10-tonne bookings to cheaper seafreight quotations.
In response to slow market conditions, he said there was now a trend amongst several other carriers serving the UK-China market to spot rate at quite low levels.
"British Airways is also quoting low whole pallet rates for the route," he said.
There are now eight days to go until the Britain's handover of Hong Kong to China.
Taiwan's EVA Air said it eagerly anticipated selling London Heathrow-HK, via Taipei, cargo flights from July 1.

"There is a lot of interest (from UK forwarders) in these HK services. We will be increasing our ex-London capacity to help cope with demand to both Taiwan and Hong Kong later this year," said EVA UK cargo spokesman Andy Whitehead.

Air China said cargo business on its recently launched weekly Heathrow-HK route had been so good that it would substitute a 40-tonne cargo capacity Boeing 747 Combi for a 12-14 tonne capacity passenger 747-400 for a month's trial from July 7.
"UK-Hong Kong is presently a very buoyant air cargo market and we would like to see the Combi switch made a permanent one," said Mac Warner, of Air China's UK cargo GSA, Pace Airline Services.
"We would be very happy to get two or three flights a week on the route and are confident we could fill the cargo space," he added.
The switch of a Combi to the HK route will mean a reduction in Air China's UK-Beijing cargo capacity.

"But this doesn't mean we are doing badly to China. We will still be offering some 70 tonnes' capacity to Beijing each week. We get good yields on the route and business in mobile 'phones, computers and general electrical equipment is encouraging," he added.
Air Hong Kong started a sixth weekly Manchester-HK 747F frequency on June 6 and UK country manager Bob Wetherill said he was pleased with booking levels.
"Despite new and anticipated competition, cargo rates to Hong Kong are holding up well," he said.
Meanwhile, EVA said its three weekly Heathrow-Bangkok-Taipei 747-400 Combi services were departing full with around 40 tonnes of freight on each flight throughout June
"We have drop-off rights at Bangkok but Taipei is our prime destination because of our onforwarding destinations available," said spokesman Whitehead.
Royal Brunei Airlines' UK cargo GSA, Ohio Express, said that on the Britain to Taipei market which RBA serves, competition was "quite intense".

Spokesman Barry McLein said that ex-London, RBA therefore preferred to concentrate on its home, oil industry influenced Brunei route and other destinations including Singapore, Malaysia, Manila, Bangkok, Darwin, Hong Kong, Jakarta and Borneo.
"From Britain, Singapore continues to hold its own in airfreight terms despite strong competition amongst carriers," he said.
"This has much to do with the continued strength of Singapore's computer industry and its need to import lots of equipment, much of it from the UK," he added.
Australia continues to suffer from over capacity but still attracts higher ex-UK yields that many Asian carriers' home markets, according to Philippine Airlines' UK cargo manager Keith O'Callaghan.

From London, the New Zealand market remains "pretty stable", said Air New Zealand's, Europe cargo manager Phil Rawlings, despite stiff competition between direct ANZ and transhipment carriers BA, MAS, KAL, EVA, Garuda and Thai International.
"Ex-UK, the NZ market has recovered from a slight decline earlier this year, with yields remaining constant," said Rawlings.
In general terms, the Middle East continues to cope with an over-abundance of capacity and frequency competition, say analysts, with Dubai suffering the most.
"Although we fly there from London, Dubai is very overcrowded with carriers and, because of the revenue factor, it is not really a market on which we focus," said Royal Brunei's McLein.

But Israel attracts a steady flow of cargo and accompanying satisfactory yields from the UK, said Andy Pape, deputy UK cargo manager of El Al, which offers 200-300 tonnes of cargo capacity a week on the route.
